newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin warns Europe on NATO, woos Belarus.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin warns Europe on NATO, woos Belarus.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin warned Europe on Thursday not to provoke Russia over NATO's eastward expansion and promised that Moscow would take a major step this year towards integration with its western neighbour Belarus.

In his annual written address to parliament, which will form the basis of a speech to be delivered on Thursday, Yeltsin said Russia would continue to seek international cooperation and, in an apparent swipe at the United States and its western allies, said no one power should be allowed world "domination".
Yeltsin repeated Russia's "profoundly negative view" of NATO's plans to expand eastward, saying it would create new divides in Europe.
"The times are getting critical for Europe," he said.
"I remind you: without Russia, and even more so against her, no one in Europe has yet been able and will ever be able to create an effective system of security."

Yeltsin reaffirmed Moscow's call for a wide-ranging treaty governing Russian-NATO relations with full legal weight and said he would work towards this in meetings with European leaders and at this month's summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton.

But the Kremlin leader, who created a Russian-Belarussian "community" last April, said further integration with the former Soviet state of 10 million which separates Russia from Poland and Lithuania would be his foreign policy priority this year.
"The most important direction for our state policy in 1997 will be Russian-Belarussian integration," he said. "This year will be a year of great new decisions for Russia and Belarus."
He did not elaborate but said both Slavic peoples had expressed their desire to "be together". He added, however, that integration should not be too hasty.

Yeltsin will meet Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko in Moscow on Friday. At least one Russian report has said the two leaders have agreed in principle to organise twin referendums this year seeking popular support for closer ties.

Moscow would certainly call the shots in any union with Belarus, a fact which is likely to cause anxiety in would-be NATO member Poland as well as in the Baltic states to the north of Belarus. It is not clear how NATO would react.

Yeltsin also said he expected closer ties with Belarus to drive integration with other former Soviet republics in the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) and, in particular, he saw ties with Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan getting closer in 1997.

On Ukraine, whose relations with Moscow have gone from bad to worse in recent months, Yeltsin called for Kiev to take a constructive approach and offered to work "patiently to solve all our problems", especially the long-running dispute over the division of the Soviet Black Sea Fleet.
Insisting Moscow had no "imperial ambitions", Yeltsin warned the former Soviet Baltic states of Estonia and Latvia not to discriminate against their large Russian-speaking minorities.
Setting out Russia's other foreign policy goals, Yeltsin said it aimed to continue to play a role in the Middle East peace process and in the Balkans.

He praised relations with China and said an expected visit by President Jiang Zemin would give "a new boost" to ties with Beijing. Elsewhere in Asia, Yeltsin said links with "friendly India" were developing, as were those with the ASEAN countries and "traditional partners" Vietnam and Mongolia.
